paras: The Bob Bridges threat against Black miners at Franklin and Newcastle was an episode reported by the Seattle Republican, a Black weekly, on 31 August 1900, in which the paper described Bob Bridges, permanent chairman of a Washington "union convention," as ready to lead the convention's delegates to kill the Black men working in the mines at Franklin and Newcastle. No violence is reported to have followed, and the item survives only as an editorial argument against Black support for Bridges.

In a paragraph among its comments on the convention, the Seattle Republican wrote that Bridges "looked just as he was ready to lead the entire delegation, 2,200 strong, to Franklin and Newcastle" and kill every Black man "at work there." The paper added, inside quotation marks and with a slur, that this would be done "even if they had to blow up the entire mines to accomplish it." The item does not say when or where during the convention the remark or display occurred, and it does not make clear whether the quoted words were Bridges's own or the editor's paraphrase.
No report of any attack on Black workers at Franklin or Newcastle appears in the coverage.

The Seattle Republican ran the item without a headline, between a jibe about Pierce and King county delegates and a mocking note on a Walla Walla delegate's speech. It closed with a direct appeal: "Are there any colored men in this state who want to support a man of that stray?" The threat thus appeared as a point in a partisan argument aimed at Black voters rather than as a news report, and no white-press account of it appears in the coverage.
